text: Here is a fundamental quality of music. <break time="0.8s" /> Note names repeat. <break time="0.8s" /> Because of a perceptual phenomenon. <break time="0.8s" /> That corresponds to the doubling and halving of frequencies. <break time="0.8s" /> When we double or halve a frequency. <break time="0.8s" /> We end up with a note. <break time="0.8s" /> That sounds remarkably similar to the one we started out with. <break time="0.8s" /> This relationship. <break time="0.8s" /> A frequency ratio of 2 to 1 or 1 to 2. <break time="0.8s" /> Is called the octave. <break time="0.8s" /> It is so important. <break time="0.8s" /> That, in spite of the large differences that exist between musical cultures. <break time="0.8s" /> Every culture we know of has the octave as the basis for its music. <break time="0.8s" /> Even if it has little else in common with other musical traditions. <break time="0.8s" /> This phenomenon leads to the notion of circularity in pitch perception. <break time="0.8s" /> And is similar to circularity in colors. <break time="0.8s" /> Although red and violet fall. <break time="0.8s" /> At opposite ends of the continuum of visible frequencies of electromagnetic energy. <break time="0.8s" /> We see them as perceptually similar. <break time="0.8s" /> The same is true in music. <break time="0.8s" /> And music is often described. <break time="0.8s" /> As having two dimensions. <break time="0.8s" /> One that accounts for tones going up in frequency. <break time="0.8s" /> And another that accounts for the perceptual sense that we have come back home again. <break time="0.8s" /> Each time we double a tones frequency.
